title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: The next day was Sunday. Stepan Arkadyevitch went to the Grand Theater for a ballet rehearsal and gave Masha Tchibisova, a pretty little dancer he had just taken under his protection, the coral necklace he had promised her the night before; in the dim daylight backstage he also managed to kiss her pretty little face, which was radiant over the gift. Besides giving her the necklace, he wanted to arrange a meeting after the ballet. He explained that he could not come at the start of the performance but promised to be there for the last act and take her to supper. From the theater Stepan Arkadyevitch drove to Ohotny Row, picked out the fish and asparagus for dinner himself, and by noon was at Dussot's, where he had three people to see — luckily all staying at the same hotel: Levin, just back from abroad and lodging there; the new head of his department, who had just been promoted to that position and had come to Moscow on a tour of inspection; and his brother-in-law Karenin, whom he had to see in order to be sure of getting him to dinner.

Stepan Arkadyevitch enjoyed dining out, but he liked even better to host a dinner — small but very select, both in the food and drink and in the choice of guests. He was especially pleased with that day's program. There would be fresh perch, asparagus, and — _la pièce de resistance_ — first-rate but plain roast beef, with wines to match: that was for the eating and drinking. Kitty and Levin would be there, and so that this would not be too obvious, there would be a girl cousin too, and young Shtcherbatsky, and — _la pièce de resistance_ among the guests — Sergey Koznishev and Alexey Alexandrovitch. Sergey Ivanovitch was a Moscow man and a philosopher; Alexey Alexandrovitch a Petersburger and a practical statesman. He had also invited the well-known eccentric enthusiast Pestsov — a liberal, a great talker, a musician, a historian, and the most charmingly youthful man of fifty you could meet — who would serve as a sauce or garnish for Koznishev and Karenin. He would needle them and set them off.

The second installment for the forest had come in from the merchant and was not yet spent; Dolly had been very pleasant and good-natured of late; and the prospect of the dinner pleased Stepan Arkadyevitch from every angle. He was in the lightest of moods. There were two slightly unpleasant things, but they were drowned in the sea of good-humored gaiety that flooded Stepan Arkadyevitch's soul. The first was that when he had met Alexey Alexandrovitch on the street the day before, he had noticed how cold and reserved his brother-in-law was with him, and putting the expression on Alexey Alexandrovitch's face, and the fact that he had not come to see them or even let them know of his arrival, together with the rumors he had heard about Anna and Vronsky, Stepan Arkadyevitch guessed that something was wrong between the husband and wife.

That was one disagreeable item. The other slightly disagreeable item was that the new head of his department, like all new heads, already had the reputation of being a terror — a man who got up at six in the morning, worked like a horse, and demanded that his subordinates do the same. On top of that, this new chief had a name for being a bear in his manners, and was, by all accounts, a man of the kind exactly opposite to that of his predecessor, the type Stepan Arkadyevitch himself had belonged to up to now. The day before, Stepan Arkadyevitch had appeared at the office in uniform, and the new chief had been very affable and had talked with him as with an old acquaintance. So Stepan Arkadyevitch felt it was his duty to call on him in plain clothes. The thought that the new chief might not give him a warm welcome was the other unpleasant point. But Stepan Arkadyevitch felt instinctively that everything would _come round_ all right. "They're all people, all men, like the rest of us poor sinners — why be nasty and quarrelsome?" he thought as he walked into the hotel.

"Good day, Vassily," he said, going down the corridor with his hat tipped to one side and addressing a footman he knew; "why, you've let your whiskers grow! Levin, number seven, right? Take me up, please. And find out whether Count Anitchkin" — this was the new chief — "is receiving."
"Yes, sir," Vassily answered, smiling. "You've not been to see us for a long while."
"I was here yesterday, but at the other entrance. Is this number seven?"
Levin was standing in the middle of the room with a peasant from Tver, measuring out a fresh bearskin, when Stepan Arkadyevitch walked in.
"What! you killed him?" Stepan Arkadyevitch cried. "Well done! A she-bear? How are you, Arhip!"
He shook hands with the peasant and sat down on the edge of a chair without taking off his coat and hat.
"Come now, take off your coat and stay a little," said Levin, taking his hat.

"No, I haven't time; I only looked in for a moment," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered. He unbuttoned his coat, but ended up taking it off after all, and sat for a whole hour talking with Levin about hunting and the most personal subjects.
"Come on, tell me, what did you do abroad? Where have you been?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked once the peasant had gone.
"Oh, I was in Germany, in Prussia, in France, and in England — not in the capitals, but in the manufacturing towns — and saw a great deal that was new to me. I'm glad I went."
"Yes, I know your idea about how to solve the labor question."

"Not at all: in Russia there can be no labor question. In Russia the question is the relation of the working people to the land; the labor question exists there too — but there it's a matter of repairing what's been ruined, while with us...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch listened to Levin attentively.

"Yes, yes!" he said. "It's very possible you're right. But I'm glad you're in good spirits, hunting bears, working, taking an interest in things. Shtcherbatsky told me another story — he met you somewhere — that you were in such a depressed state, talking of nothing but death...."

"Well, what of it? I haven't given up thinking of death," Levin said. "It's true that it's high time I was dead, and that all this is nonsense. I'm telling you the truth. I really do value my idea and my work; but in reality just consider this: our whole world is nothing but a speck of mildew that has grown up on a tiny planet. And for us to suppose we can have anything great — ideas, work — it's all dust and ashes."
"But all that's as old as the hills, my boy!"

"It is old, but you know, once you really take it in, then somehow everything becomes meaningless. Once you grasp that you'll die tomorrow if not today, and nothing will be left, then everything is so trivial! I think my idea is very important, but it turns out to be just as trivial, even if it were carried out, as that bear-killing business. So one goes on living — amusing oneself with hunting, with work — anything to avoid thinking of death!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled a subtle, affectionate smile as he listened to Levin.
"Well, of course! Now you've come round to my point of view. Remember how you used to attack me for chasing enjoyment in life? Don't be so hard on us, O moralist!"
"No; all the same, what's fine in life is...." Levin hesitated — "oh, I don't know. All I know is that we'll soon be dead."
"Why so soon?"
"And you know, life has less charm once you think of death — but more peace."
"On the contrary, the end is always the best part. But I really must go," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, getting up for the tenth time.
"Oh, no, stay a little longer!" Levin said, holding him back. "When will we see each other again? I leave tomorrow."
"What an idiot I am! That's exactly what I came for! You absolutely must come to dinner with us today. Your brother is coming, and Karenin, my brother-in-law."

"You don't mean to say he's here?" Levin said, and was on the point of asking about Kitty. He had heard at the start of the winter that she was in Petersburg with her sister, the diplomat's wife, and he did not know whether she had come back; but he changed his mind and did not ask. "Whether she's coming or not, I don't care," he told himself.
"So you'll come?"
"Of course."
"Five o'clock, then, and no evening dress."

And Stepan Arkadyevitch got up and went downstairs to see the new head of his department. His instinct had not misled him. The terrifying new chief turned out to be an extremely agreeable man, and Stepan Arkadyevitch had lunch with him and stayed on, so that it was four o'clock by the time he got to Alexey Alexandrovitch.
